core_claim.quote: In the limit, one can think of each and every conscious experience as (phenomenologically) integrating multimodal bodily and environmental signals in the service of coordinating allostatic regulation and survival-relevant action

source.citation: Seth AK. Conscious artificial intelligence and biological naturalism. Behavioral and Brain Sciences 49, e315 (published online 2025-04-21)

prediction.statement: The sense of presence (that oneself and the world are real and here) is strongest when the body's actual signals match what the brain predicted them to be; making those predictions imprecise lowers presence, while simply raising the mismatch raises anxiety instead.

first_stated.passage: The core concept of the model is that a sense of presence arises when informative interoceptive prediction signals are successfully matched to inputs so that prediction errors are suppressed.

source.citation: Seth AK, Suzuki K, Critchley HD. An interoceptive predictive coding model of conscious presence. Frontiers in Psychology 2:395 (2011 volume)

prediction.test_for: When people's expectations of how their body will respond are manipulated, presence is higher when what they then feel matches what they expected, and lower when it does not, in either direction.
prediction.test_against: Presence does not depend on the match between expected and felt bodily response, or a mismatch in one direction raises presence as reliably as a match does.

other_statements_of_the_prediction.passage: A basic prediction of the model is that artificially induced imprecision in interoceptive predictions should lead to diminished conscious presence and abnormal AIC activity; by contrast, simple elevation of interoceptive prediction error signals should lead instead to increased anxiety.

source.citation: Seth AK, Suzuki K, Critchley HD. An interoceptive predictive coding model of conscious presence. Frontiers in Psychology 2:395 (2011 volume)

other_statements_of_the_prediction.passage: Manipulations of top-down expectations could be achieved by modifying the context in which subjects are tested.
